To lowball means to deliberately give someone a number — a price, a quote, an estimate, an offer — that is intentionally lower than what is realistic or truthful, usually to gain an advantage.

The key word is deliberately. When you lowball, you aren't making an honest mistake. You are either lying, or you know the real number will be higher, but you quote a low number on purpose to win someone over first.
How It Works in Real Life

The classic setting is a negotiation or a transaction — anything where numbers are exchanged.

Example 1 — A contractor lowballs a quote:
You ask a renovation company how much it will cost to renovate your kitchen. They know the realistic cost is ₹8 lakhs, but they quote you ₹4 lakhs to win your business. After you hire them and work begins, they keep adding "unexpected" costs — materials, labour, delays — and the final bill ends up being ₹9 lakhs anyway. That initial ₹4 lakh quote was a lowball.

Example 2 — A used car dealer lowballs your trade-in:
You bring your old car to a dealer, hoping to trade it in. The car is genuinely worth ₹3 lakhs. The dealer tells you it's only worth ₹1.5 lakhs — lowballing your car's value so they pay you less and make more profit.

Example 3 — A company lowballs a salary offer:
A company wants to hire you. They know the market rate for your role is ₹15 LPA, and they're willing to pay that, but their first offer is ₹10 LPA. They lowballed you, hoping you'll simply accept without negotiating.

Lowballing almost always serves one of two goals:

  1. To win a deal or a contract — by quoting low, you look more attractive than competitors. Once you've got the person committed, you recover your margins later through extra charges, revised terms, or simple pressure.
  2. To pay less / get more — by undervaluing what the other person is offering (their car, their skills, their product), you shift the deal in your favour.

This is why lowballing carries a negative, slightly dishonest connotation. It's not aggressive lying — it's more like strategic misleading. The person being lowballed makes a decision based on a false picture of reality.
The "Lowball Technique" — A Known Manipulation Tactic

In sales and psychology, lowballing refers to a specific manipulation pattern that works like this:

  1. You offer someone a great deal at a very attractive low number.
  2. They say yes and mentally commit.
  3. After they've agreed, you reveal that the original number was wrong, incomplete, or that there are additional costs.
  4. Because they've already said yes and are mentally invested, most people still go through with it rather than backing out.

This works because of human psychology: once we've made a decision, we tend to stick with it even when the terms change. The lowballer exploits this.

Outside of deliberate manipulation, people sometimes use "lowball" more casually to mean underestimate, without implying dishonesty:

"I lowballed how long the project would take — I said two weeks, but it took six."

Here, the speaker is admitting their own estimate was too low — not necessarily on purpose. This is a softer, more self-aware use of the word. Context will usually tell you whether someone is confessing to deception or simply admitting a misjudgement.

A seller can lowball the value of something you own (to pay you less). A contractor can lowball their bid (to beat competitors and win the work). An employer can lowball a salary offer (to hire you cheap). An estimator can lowball a timeline or budget (to seem more attractive or capable than they are).
How to Use It in a Sentence

• "Don't let them lowball you — your work is worth much more."
  • "The mechanic lowballed the repair cost to get me through the door."
  • "I think I lowballed my budget estimate. It's going to cost more."
  • "She lowballed her initial bid to win the contract, planning to negotiate upward later."

The opposite of lowball is highball — to give a deliberately high estimate or offer, typically to leave room to negotiate down, or to make a later compromise look like a concession. Together, lowballing and highballing are two of the most common opening moves in any negotiation.

To lowball is to put a dishonestly or unrealistically low number on the table — a price, an offer, an estimate — for strategic gain. It's a move that makes you look cheaper, more generous, or more capable than you actually are. The person on the receiving end of a lowball makes decisions based on misleading information, which is exactly what the lowballer intends.
